title: Ἱππόδρομος
about: The horsemen gather at Achilles’ word, and the poet names the five drivers with their horses as they come forward: Eumelus, Diomedes with the horses he once took from Aeneas, Menelaus with Aethe and Podargus, Antilochus with his Pylos-born team, and Meriones. Before the start, Nestor draws Antilochus aside and tells him that his horses are the slowest, so he must win by cunning: the woodcutter, the helmsman and the charioteer all do better by skill than by force. He describes the dry turning-post with its two white stones, tells his son to lean left, goad the right-hand horse and hug the post without touching the stone, and then sits down. They draw lots for places, Achilles marks the turning-points and seats Phoenix as a witness, and the five teams burst off across the plain in a cloud of dust, manes streaming, chariots leaping, each driver calling to his horses.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο Πηλεΐδης, ταχέες δ’ ἱππῆες ἄγερθεν.
sentences.l: So spoke Peleus’-son, and the swift horsemen gathered.
sentences.i: So spoke the son of Peleus, and the swift horsemen gathered.
sentences.n: The part opens on the formula that closes Achilles’ speech from the previous part. φάτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of φημί ‘say’, and Πηλεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Peleus’, here standing for Achilles. ἱππῆες ‘horsemen’ is the usual epic word for men who drive chariots, and ἄγερθεν is the aorist passive of ἀγείρω ‘gather’ with no augment and the ending -εν for -ησαν: the drivers who want to race come forward.

sentences.t:
ὦρτο πολὺ πρῶτος μὲν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Εὔμηλος
Ἀδμήτου φίλος υἱός, ὃς ἱπποσύνῃ ἐκέκαστο·
sentences.l:
Rose by far the first the lord of men, Eumelus,
Admetus’ dear son, who in horsemanship had excelled;
sentences.i: By far the first to rise was the lord of men, Eumelus, Admetus’ dear son, who excelled in horsemanship;
sentences.n: The five drivers rise one by one, and the poet names each with his horses. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, ‘rose, started up’, with the augment fused into the stem. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock phrase, translated every time, though it is more often said of Agamemnon; line 288 repeats, with a different name, a line of an earlier part that opens a rise of drivers with Agamemnon. ἱπποσύνῃ is a dative of respect, ‘in horsemanship’, and ἐκέκαστο is the pluperfect of the old verb καίνυμαι ‘excel’, which has a simple past sense.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ Τυδεΐδης ὦρτο κρατερὸς Διομήδης,
ἵππους δὲ Τρῳοὺς ὕπαγε ζυγόν, οὕς ποτ’ ἀπηύρα
Αἰνείαν, ἀτὰρ αὐτὸν ὑπεξεσάωσεν Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.l:
and after him rose the son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes,
and the Trojan horses he led under the yoke, which once he took away from
Aeneas, but himself Apollo rescued from under.
sentences.i: and after him rose the son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes, bringing under the yoke the Trojan horses that he had once taken from Aeneas, though Apollo had rescued Aeneas himself.
sentences.n: Line 290 is word for word a line of the same earlier part, where Diomedes rises after Agamemnon; τῷ δ’ ἐπί means ‘and after him’. Τυδεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Tydeus’ and κρατερὸς Διομήδης ‘strong Diomedes’ is the stock pair. ὕπαγε ζυγόν is ‘led under the yoke’, and ἀπηύρα is the aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take away from’, with Αἰνείαν as the man robbed. The story of how Diomedes won Aeneas’ horses is told earlier, in Book 5. ὑπεξεσάωσεν is ‘rescued out from under’, with the compound formed of three parts (ὑπό, ἐκ, σαόω), and αὐτόν ‘himself’ is Aeneas.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ Ἀτρεΐδης ὦρτο ξανθὸς Μενέλαος
διογενής, ὑπὸ δὲ ζυγὸν ἤγαγεν ὠκέας ἵππους
Αἴθην τὴν Ἀγαμεμνονέην τὸν ἑόν τε Πόδαργον·
sentences.i: and after him rose the son of Atreus, fair-haired Menelaus, Zeus-born, and he put swift horses under the yoke: Agamemnon’s mare Aethe and his own Podargus;
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ again means ‘and after him’, and Ἀτρεΐδης is the patronymic, here for Menelaus. ξανθὸς Μενέλαος ‘fair-haired Menelaus’ and διογενής ‘Zeus-sprung’ (‘Zeus-born’ in i) are stock epithets, translated every time; the second stands after its noun, across the line break. ὑπὸ … ἤγαγεν is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb, and means ‘led under (the yoke)’. Αἴθην, in apposition to ὠκέας ἵππους, is a mare’s name, and the adjective Ἀγαμεμνονέην means ‘of Agamemnon’. Πόδαργος is a horse’s name, and ἑόν ‘his own’ is the possessive, not a relative.

sentences.t:
τὴν Ἀγαμέμνονι δῶκ’ Ἀγχισιάδης Ἐχέπωλος
δῶρ’, ἵνα μή οἱ ἕποιθ’ ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν,
ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ τέρποιτο μένων·
sentences.i: Echepolus, son of Anchises, had given her to Agamemnon as a gift, so that he would not have to follow him to windy Ilios, but could stay where he was and take his pleasure;
sentences.n: τήν ‘her’ is Aethe. δῶκ’ is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι, with δῶρ’ ‘as a gift’, and Ἀγχισιάδης is the patronymic ‘son of Anchises’. ἵνα μή with the optative ἕποιθ’ (ἕποιτο from ἕπομαι ‘follow’; the τ becomes θ before the rough breathing of ὑπό) gives the purpose in past time; οἱ ‘him’ is Agamemnon, and the one who stays behind is Echepolus. Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν ‘windy Ilios’ is a stock phrase. αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot, right there’, and τέρποιτο is the optative of τέρπομαι ‘take pleasure’. So the mare was the price of staying at home.

sentences.t:
μέγα γάρ οἱ ἔδωκε
Ζεὺς ἄφενος, ναῖεν δ’ ὅ γ’ ἐν εὐρυχόρῳ Σικυῶνι·
sentences.l:
for greatly to him gave
Zeus wealth, and he dwelt in Sicyon of wide dancing-grounds;
sentences.i: for Zeus had given him great wealth, and he lived in spacious Sicyon;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason Echepolus could afford to stay at home: οἱ ‘to him’ is Echepolus now. μέγα is neuter and can be taken as an adverb, ‘greatly’ (so in l), or with ἄφενος as ‘great’ (so in i); ἄφενος is ‘wealth’. ναῖεν is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, and ὅ γ’ ‘he’ points back to Echepolus. εὐρυχόρῳ is the stock epithet of Sicyon, translated ‘of wide dancing-grounds’ in l and ‘spacious’ in i, as the Odyssey does, with χόρος taken as a dancing-floor or open space.

sentences.t: τὴν ὅ γ’ ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ἦγε μέγα δρόμου ἰσχανόωσαν.
sentences.l: her he under the yoke led, greatly longing for the running.
sentences.i: He put her under the yoke, a mare greatly eager for the race.
sentences.n: τήν is Aethe again, and ὅ γ’ is Menelaus, who yokes her. ἰσχανόωσαν is a feminine participle (diectasis, Attic ἰσχανῶσαν) of the rare verb ἰσχανάω, which is usually taken to mean ‘be eager for, long for’ with the genitive δρόμου ‘the running, the race’; the exact sense is uncertain. μέγα ‘greatly’ goes with it.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δὲ τέταρτος ἐΰτριχας ὁπλίσαθ’ ἵππους,
Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱὸς ὑπερθύμοιο ἄνακτος
τοῦ Νηληϊάδαο·
sentences.i: Fourth, Antilochus made ready his well-maned horses, the splendid son of Nestor, the high-spirited lord, Neleus’ son;
sentences.n: Antilochus is the fourth to come forward, as τέταρτος says. ὁπλίσαθ’ is the aorist middle of ὁπλίζω ‘make ready’, here the horses; ἐΰτριχας is ‘well-maned’, as at 23.13. ἀγλαὸς υἱός ‘splendid son’ and ὑπερθύμοιο ‘high-spirited’ are stock words, ἄνακτος ‘lord’ is said of Nestor, and τοῦ Νηληϊάδαο is a second description, ‘him, Neleus’ son’, a patronymic with the genitive ending -αο.

sentences.t:
Πυλοιγενέες δέ οἱ ἵπποι
ὠκύποδες φέρον ἅρμα·
sentences.l:
and Pylos-born for him the horses,
swift-footed, bore the chariot;
sentences.i: and his horses, born at Pylos and swift-footed, were bearing the chariot;
sentences.n: Πυλοιγενέες is a compound, ‘born at Pylos’ (Nestor’s city), and is nominative plural, agreeing with ἵπποι ‘horses’. ὠκύποδες ‘swift-footed’ is the table’s rendering of the epithet. φέρον is the imperfect, ‘were carrying’, with ἅρμα ‘chariot’. οἱ ‘for him’ is Antilochus.

sentences.t:
πατὴρ δέ οἱ ἄγχι παραστὰς
μυθεῖτ’ εἰς ἀγαθὰ φρονέων νοέοντι καὶ αὐτῷ·
sentences.l:
and his father, standing close by,
spoke, with good in mind, to him who also himself had understanding:
sentences.i: and his father, standing close beside him, spoke to him with kindly intent, to one who himself had understanding as well:
sentences.n: πατήρ is Nestor, who will now give advice at length (the speech runs to line 348). παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’, and ἄγχι παραστάς ‘standing close by’ is a formula. μυθεῖτ’ is the imperfect of μυθέομαι ‘speak’. εἰς ἀγαθὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking toward good things’, that is, with kind intent, and νοέοντι καὶ αὐτῷ is ‘to one who himself also thought (understood)’: Nestor is about to advise a son who already has some skill.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχ’ ἤτοι μέν σε νέον περ ἐόντ’ ἐφίλησαν
Ζεύς τε Ποσειδάων τε, καὶ ἱπποσύνας ἐδίδαξαν
παντοίας·
sentences.i: “Antilochus, Zeus and Poseidon loved you, young though you are, and taught you horsemanship of every kind;
sentences.n: Nestor’s speech begins. Ἀντίλοχ’ is the vocative. ἤτοι μέν ‘indeed’ (the edition prints ἤτοι as one word) sets up the contrast that comes with ἀλλά in line 309, and νέον περ ἐόντ’ is ‘though being young’. ἐφίλησαν is the aorist ‘loved’, with the two gods as subject (Ζεύς τε Ποσειδάων τε, in epic -ων for Attic Ποσειδῶν). ἱπποσύνας is the plural of ἱπποσύνη ‘horsemanship’, ‘the skills of a horseman’, and παντοίας ‘of every kind’ ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t: τὼ καί σε διδασκέμεν οὔ τι μάλα χρεώ·
sentences.l: therefore also to teach you there is not much need;
sentences.i: so there is not much need to teach you as well;
sentences.n: τώ here, printed τὼ, is the adverb ‘therefore’ (an old form of τῷ), not the dual article. καί σε is ‘you also’, after the gods who have already taught him. διδασκέμεν is the epic infinitive in -έμεν (= διδάσκειν), and χρεώ is an indeclinable noun ‘need’, used with an understood ‘is’: οὔ τι μάλα χρεώ ‘there is not much need at all’.

sentences.t: οἶσθα γὰρ εὖ περὶ τέρμαθ’ ἑλισσέμεν·
sentences.l: for you know well how to wheel round the turning-posts;
sentences.i: for you know well how to turn around the turning-posts;
sentences.n: οἶσθα is the perfect of οἶδα ‘know’, with the infinitive ‘know how to’. τέρμαθ’ is the plural of τέρμα, the post at the end of the course that the chariots turn round, ‘turning-post’. ἑλισσέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἑλίσσω ‘turn, wheel’. περί with the accusative means ‘round’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τοι ἵπποι
βάρδιστοι θείειν·
sentences.l:
but to you the horses
are slowest to run;
sentences.i: but your horses are the slowest runners;
sentences.n: ἀλλά τοι ἵπποι: τοι is the Homeric form of σοι ‘to you’, so ‘your horses’. βάρδιστοι is the superlative of βραδύς ‘slow’, and θείειν is the epic form of the infinitive θεῖν ‘to run’. The Greek says ‘slowest to run’, and Nestor will not soften it.

sentences.t: τώ τ’ οἴω λοίγι’ ἔσεσθαι.
sentences.l: therefore I think there will be disastrous things.
sentences.i: so I think there will be disaster.
sentences.n: τώ τ’ is again ‘therefore’ with an enclitic τε that adds nothing. οἴω is ὀΐω ‘I think, suppose’, and the infinitive ἔσεσθαι is the future of εἰμί ‘be’. λοίγι’ is the neuter plural λοίγια ‘disastrous things’, from the adjective λοίγιος ‘ruinous’ (from λοιγός ‘ruin’).

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἵπποι μὲν ἔασιν ἀφάρτεροι, οὐδὲ μὲν αὐτοὶ
πλείονα ἴσασιν σέθεν αὐτοῦ μητίσασθαι.
sentences.l:
But of those the horses are swifter, and yet they themselves
know no more than you yourself how to plan.
sentences.i: Their horses are swifter, but the men themselves know no more than you yourself about how to plan.
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of those’ means the other drivers, who are not named. ἀφάρτεροι is a comparative, ‘swifter’. The sense turns on οὐδὲ μέν ‘and yet not’: the other men have no more mind than Antilochus. ἴσασιν is the 3rd plural of οἶδα ‘know’, with πλείονα ‘more’ and σέθεν αὐτοῦ ‘than you yourself’ (σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ, and a genitive of comparison). μητίσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of μητίομαι ‘plan’, from μῆτις ‘cunning’, the word that carries Nestor’s argument.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ σὺ φίλος μῆτιν ἐμβάλλεο θυμῷ
παντοίην, ἵνα μή σε παρεκπροφύγῃσιν ἄεθλα.
sentences.l:
But come now, you, dear, put cunning in your heart
of every kind, so that the contest-prizes not slip past you.
sentences.i: But come now, my friend, put cunning of every kind into your heart, so that the prizes do not slip past you.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’. φίλος ‘dear’ is a nominative with the force of an address, and μῆτιν ‘cunning’ is the word Nestor will keep returning to. ἐμβάλλεο is the epic imperative middle of ἐμβάλλω ‘put into’, and θυμῷ ‘heart’ is the dative. ἵνα μή with the subjunctive παρεκπροφύγῃσιν (a compound ‘slip past and away’, with the epic ending -ῃσιν) gives the purpose, and ἄεθλα are the ‘contest-prizes’ (‘prizes’ in i) of the race.

sentences.t: μήτι τοι δρυτόμος μέγ’ ἀμείνων ἠὲ βίηφι·
sentences.l: By cunning the woodcutter is far better than by strength;
sentences.i: By cunning a woodcutter is far better than by strength;
sentences.n: Three of the next four lines (315, 316, 318) begin with μήτι, the dative of μῆτις ‘cunning’, ‘by cunning’, and give three examples. τοι is ‘you see’, a particle here. δρυτόμος ‘woodcutter’ is a compound of δρῦς ‘oak’ and the root of τέμνω ‘cut’. ἀμείνων is ‘better’, and βίηφι is the old instrumental ‘by strength’.

sentences.t:
μήτι δ’ αὖτε κυβερνήτης ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ
νῆα θοὴν ἰθύνει ἐρεχθομένην ἀνέμοισι·
sentences.l:
By cunning in turn a helmsman on the wine-faced open-sea
steers a swift ship, battered by winds;
sentences.i: By cunning a helmsman on the sea that has the look of wine steers a swift ship, though winds batter her;
sentences.n: μήτι δ’ αὖτε ‘and by cunning in turn’ is the second example. κυβερνήτης is ‘helmsman’. οἴνοπι πόντῳ is the stock phrase for the sea, ‘wine-faced open-sea’ in l and ‘the sea that has the look of wine’ in i, the table’s rendering. ἰθύνει is the present of ἰθύνω ‘make straight, steer’, and ἐρεχθομένην is a passive participle of ἐρέχθω, ‘being battered’, with ἀνέμοισι ‘by winds’. νῆα θοήν ‘swift ship’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t: μήτι δ’ ἡνίοχος περιγίγνεται ἡνιόχοιο.
sentences.l: By cunning charioteer surpasses charioteer.
sentences.i: By cunning one charioteer surpasses another.
sentences.n: The third example, and the one that comes home. περιγίγνεται is ‘be superior to’, with the genitive ἡνιόχοιο ‘than the (other) charioteer’; ἡνίοχος is the driver, the man who holds the ἡνία ‘reins’. The Greek puts the same word twice, ‘charioteer’ over ‘charioteer’, and l keeps that.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃς μέν θ’ ἵπποισι καὶ ἅρμασιν οἷσι πεποιθὼς
ἀφραδέως ἐπὶ πολλὸν ἑλίσσεται ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα,
ἵπποι δὲ πλανόωνται ἀνὰ δρόμον, οὐδὲ κατίσχει·
sentences.i: But the man who trusts in his own horses and chariot and swings senselessly wide, this way and that, while his horses wander over the course and he cannot hold them in;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὃς μέν θ’ begins a relative clause that is never given a main verb: after ‘the man who … wheels’ the sentence runs on in plain statements, ‘and his horses stray, and he does not hold them’, and the contrast comes with ὃς δέ κε in line 322. οἷσι is the possessive ‘his own’ (dative plural), not a relative pronoun, and πεποιθώς is the perfect participle of πείθομαι ‘trust’. ἅρμασι is plural for one chariot. ἀφραδέως ‘senselessly’; ἐπὶ πολλόν ‘over a great space’; ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ‘this way and that’. πλανόωνται is the diectasis form of πλανῶνται ‘wander’, and κατίσχει ‘holds back’ has the driver as subject.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κε κέρδεα εἰδῇ ἐλαύνων ἥσσονας ἵππους,
αἰεὶ τέρμ’ ὁρόων στρέφει ἐγγύθεν, οὐδέ ἑ λήθει
ὅππως τὸ πρῶτον τανύσῃ βοέοισιν ἱμᾶσιν,
ἀλλ’ ἔχει ἀσφαλέως καὶ τὸν προὔχοντα δοκεύει.
sentences.l:
But whoever knows the gains, driving lesser horses,
always looking at the post turns close by, and it does not escape him
how at the first he is to pull taut with the oxhide straps,
but he holds them steadily and watches the one who is ahead.
sentences.i: But the man who knows how to gain an advantage, though driving the lesser horses, always keeps his eye on the post and turns close to it, and it does not escape him how to pull taut with the oxhide straps at the first, but he holds them steady and watches the man who is ahead.
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κε εἰδῇ is a general relative clause, ‘whoever knows’, with the subjunctive. κέρδεα ‘gains’ here means the points of advantage a clever driver finds; ἥσσονας ‘lesser’ is the comparative ἥσσων. ὁρόων is the diectasis form of ὁρῶν, and στρέφει ‘turns’ has ἐγγύθεν ‘close by’. οὐδέ ἑ λήθει is ‘it does not escape him’, with ἑ ‘him’ as object and the ὅππως ‘how’ clause as subject. The exact sense of τὸ πρῶτον τανύσῃ ‘pull taut at the first’ is disputed. ἱμᾶσιν ‘straps’ are the leather reins. ἔχει ‘holds’ has the reins or the team as an understood object, and τὸν προὔχοντα is ‘the one going ahead’ (crasis of προέχοντα).

sentences.t: σῆμα δέ τοι ἐρέω μάλ’ ἀριφραδές, οὐδέ σε λήσει.
sentences.l: And a sign to you I will tell, very plain, and it will not escape you.
sentences.i: And I will tell you a sign, very plain, that will not escape you.
sentences.n: The edition prints a full stop here; the same words stand in the Odyssey, where they end in a colon, and the English is that line’s with the stop changed. σῆμα is ‘sign, mark’, and the sign is the post described in the next lines. ἐρέω is the epic future of λέγω ‘tell’, and ἀριφραδές ‘very plain’ is an adjective whose prefix ἀρι- is intensive. οὐδέ σε λήσει is ‘it will not escape you’, the same verb as λήθει three lines above.

sentences.t:
ἕστηκε ξύλον αὖον ὅσον τ’ ὄργυι’ ὑπὲρ αἴης
ἢ δρυὸς ἢ πεύκης·
sentences.l:
There stands a dry piece of wood, about a fathom above the ground,
either of oak or of pine;
sentences.i: A dry piece of wood stands there, about a fathom above the ground, either of oak or of pine;
sentences.n: ἕστηκε is the perfect of ἵστημι, ‘stands’, and ξύλον αὖον ‘dry piece of wood’ is the mark Nestor describes, a mark on the course. ὅσον τ’ ὄργυι’ ‘as much as a fathom’ uses ὄργυια, the length of a man’s outstretched arms, about six feet. αἴης is the Ionic form of αἶα ‘earth’ (= γαίης). ἢ … ἢ ‘either … or’ names the wood: oak (δρῦς) or pine (πεύκη).

sentences.t:
τὸ μὲν οὐ καταπύθεται ὄμβρῳ,
λᾶε δὲ τοῦ ἑκάτερθεν ἐρηρέδαται δύο λευκὼ
ἐν ξυνοχῇσιν ὁδοῦ, λεῖος δ’ ἱππόδρομος ἀμφὶς,
sentences.l:
it does not rot in the rain,
and two white stones on either side of it are fixed
at the meetings of the track, and smooth the horse-course all round,
sentences.i: it does not rot in the rain, and on either side of it two white stones are fixed where the track meets, and the racecourse all round is smooth,
sentences.n: τὸ μέν ‘it, for its part’ is the wood, and καταπύθεται is the present of καταπύθομαι ‘rot away’ with ὄμβρῳ ‘in the rain’. λᾶε … λευκώ is a dual, ‘two stones, two white ones’ (nominative of λᾶας), with the plural verb ἐρηρέδαται, the perfect passive of ἐρείδω ‘prop, fix’. τοῦ ἑκάτερθεν is ‘on either side of it’. ξυνοχῇσιν ὁδοῦ is ‘at the junctions of the way’: the picture, whether the track narrows or meets here, is not certain. ἱππόδρομος is the ‘horse-course’, and ἀμφίς ‘all round’. The edition’s text, as archived, lacked the comma after ἀμφὶς; it is added here (README rule 5), and the sentence goes on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἤ τευ σῆμα βροτοῖο πάλαι κατατεθνηῶτος,
ἢ τό γε νύσσα τέτυκτο ἐπὶ προτέρων ἀνθρώπων,
καὶ νῦν τέρματ’ ἔθηκε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l:
either some mortal’s grave-mark, long dead,
or it was a turning-point in the time of men before,
and now the turning-posts swift-footed, heavenly Achilles has set.
sentences.i: either the grave-mark of some mortal long dead, or it was a turning-point in the days of men before us, and now swift-footed, heavenly Achilles has made it his turning-post.
sentences.n: The two ἤ clauses give what the old wood might be: a σῆμα, here a grave-marker, of some man long dead, or a νύσσα ‘turning-point’ in the time of earlier men. τευ is the Ionic form of τινος ‘of some’, and κατατεθνηῶτος is the perfect participle of καταθνῄσκω ‘die’ with the epic -ηῶτ-. ἐπὶ προτέρων ἀνθρώπων is ‘in the time of earlier men’, and τέτυκτο is the pluperfect of τεύχω ‘make’. The plural τέρματ’ is ‘turning-posts’, as at line 309, though the post is one; ἔθηκε is ‘has made, set up’. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is the stock epithet pair ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’. The formation of ποδάρκης is uncertain (probably πούς + ἀρκέω).

sentences.t:
τῷ σὺ μάλ’ ἐγχρίμψας ἐλάαν σχεδὸν ἅρμα καὶ ἵππους,
αὐτὸς δὲ κλινθῆναι ἐϋπλέκτῳ ἐνὶ δίφρῳ
ἦκ’ ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ τοῖιν·
sentences.i: Press in very close to it, drive your chariot and horses near, and lean over in your well-woven chariot a little to the left of the pair;
sentences.n: τῷ ‘to it’ is the post. ἐγχρίμψας is the aorist participle of ἐγχρίμπτω ‘press close’, and ἐλάαν and κλινθῆναι are infinitives used as commands (the epic ἐλάαν = ἐλαύνειν, and κλινθῆναι the aorist passive of κλίνω ‘lean’), as is κένσαι in the next unit. ἐϋπλέκτῳ ‘well-woven’ is said of the chariot. ἦκ’ is ἦκα ‘gently, a little’. τοῖιν is a dual genitive, ‘of the two’ (the two horses), with ἐπ’ ἀριστερά ‘to the left’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ τὸν δεξιὸν ἵππον
κένσαι ὁμοκλήσας, εἶξαί τέ οἱ ἡνία χερσίν.
sentences.l:
but the right-hand horse
prick, shouting at him, and yield to him the reins with your hands.
sentences.i: but goad the right-hand horse, shouting at him, and slacken the reins in your hands for him.
sentences.n: κένσαι is the aorist infinitive of κεντέω ‘prick, goad’, used as a command. ὁμοκλήσας is the aorist participle of ὁμοκλάω ‘shout at’, and the stock verb stays ‘shout at’. εἶξαι is the aorist infinitive of εἴκω ‘give way’, so εἶξαί τέ οἱ ἡνία χερσίν takes ἡνία as its object, ‘yield him the reins with your hands’, that is, let the reins go slack for the horse. The inside horse is held in; the outside horse is driven on.

sentences.t:
ἐν νύσσῃ δέ τοι ἵππος ἀριστερὸς ἐγχριμφθήτω,
ὡς ἄν τοι πλήμνη γε δοάσσεται ἄκρον ἱκέσθαι
κύκλου ποιητοῖο·
sentences.i: And at the turning-point let the left-hand horse be pressed in close, so that the hub will seem to you to reach the rim of the well-made wheel;
sentences.n: νύσσα here is the turning-point, the same as the post; ἐγχριμφθήτω is the aorist passive imperative of ἐγχρίμπτω, ‘let it be pressed close’. ὡς ἄν with δοάσσεται, ‘it may seem’, gives the aim, ‘so that’. πλήμνη is the ‘nave’, the hub of the wheel, and ἄκρον κύκλου is ‘the edge of the wheel’. The picture is of the wheel running so close to the post that it seems about to graze it; exactly how the Greek gets there is disputed. τοι is again ‘to you’, and ποιητοῖο ‘well-made’ is ‘made, fashioned’ (of the wheel).

sentences.t:
λίθου δ’ ἀλέασθαι ἐπαυρεῖν,
μή πως ἵππους τε τρώσῃς κατά θ’ ἅρματα ἄξῃς·
sentences.l:
and the stone to avoid touching,
lest somehow you wound the horses and break the chariot;
sentences.i: but take care not to touch the stone, or you may somehow wound your horses and break your chariot;
sentences.n: λίθου ‘the stone’ is one of the two white λᾶε of line 329, and ἀλέασθαι ‘avoid’ and ἐπαυρεῖν ‘touch, come against’ are both infinitives used as commands, with the genitive after ἐπαυρεῖν. μή πως with the subjunctive means ‘lest somehow’: τρώσῃς is the aorist of τιτρώσκω ‘wound’, and κατὰ … ἄξῃς is tmesis for κατάξῃς, ‘break’ (the aorist subjunctive of κατάγνυμι). ἅρματα is plural for one chariot.

sentences.t:
χάρμα δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοισιν, ἐλεγχείη δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ
ἔσσεται·
sentences.l:
and a joy to the others, but a disgrace to yourself
it will be;
sentences.i: and it will be a joy to the others, but a disgrace to you yourself;
sentences.n: χάρμα ‘a joy’ is said of what the rivals will feel, and ἐλεγχείη is ‘disgrace, reproach’. ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί (Attic ἔσται). σοὶ αὐτῷ is ‘to you yourself’. The unit ends in the middle of line 343.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ φίλος φρονέων πεφυλαγμένος εἶναι.
sentences.l: But, dear, being thoughtful, be on your guard.
sentences.i: But, my friend, be thoughtful and be on your guard.
sentences.n: φίλος is again a nominative serving as an address, and φρονέων is ‘thinking, using sense’. πεφυλαγμένος εἶναι is the perfect passive participle of φυλάσσω ‘guard’ with the infinitive of εἰμί used as a command, ‘be guarded’.

sentences.t:
εἰ γάρ κ’ ἐν νύσσῃ γε παρεξελάσῃσθα διώκων,
οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὅς κέ σ’ ἕλῃσι μετάλμενος οὐδὲ παρέλθῃ,
sentences.l:
For if at the turning-point you drive past, pursuing,
there is no one who could catch you, leaping after, nor go past you,
sentences.i: For if you drive past the others at the turning-point as you race, there is no one who could leap after you and catch you, or get by you,
sentences.n: εἰ γάρ κ’ with the aorist subjunctive παρεξελάσῃσθα (epic 2nd singular -σθα, ‘drive past’) is an open condition, and διώκων is ‘pursuing’, here ‘racing, in the chase’. οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὅς κε is ‘there is no one who’, and ἕλῃσι and παρέλθῃ are subjunctives (the first with the epic ending -ῃσι) with μετάλμενος, the aorist middle participle of μεθάλλομαι ‘leap after’. The sentence continues into the next unit, which Nestor uses for his strongest case.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ κεν μετόπισθεν Ἀρίονα δῖον ἐλαύνοι
Ἀδρήστου ταχὺν ἵππον, ὃς ἐκ θεόφιν γένος ἦεν,
ἢ τοὺς Λαομέδοντος, οἳ ἐνθάδε γ’ ἔτραφεν ἐσθλοί.
sentences.l:
not even if behind he were driving heavenly Arion,
the swift horse of Adrastus, who in race was from gods,
or those of Laomedon, who here were reared, good ones.”
sentences.i: not even if someone behind you were driving heavenly Arion, the swift horse of Adrastus, a horse of divine stock, or the good horses of Laomedon, which were reared here.”
sentences.n: οὐδ’ εἴ κεν with the optative ἐλαύνοι is ‘not even if he were driving’. Ἀρίων is a famous horse, and the epithet δῖον ‘heavenly’ is said of him; the phrase ὃς ἐκ θεόφιν γένος ἦεν is ‘who was in birth from gods’, with θεόφιν an old ending that marks source (‘from gods’, number not marked). τοὺς Λαομέδοντος ‘those of Laomedon’ means the horses, and ἐνθάδε ‘here’ means in the land of Troy; ἔτραφεν is the aorist passive of τρέφω in the plural sense, ‘were reared’. Nestor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν Νέστωρ Νηλήϊος ἂψ ἐνὶ χώρῃ
ἕζετ’, ἐπεὶ ᾧ παιδὶ ἑκάστου πείρατ’ ἔειπε.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, Nestor the Neleian back in his place
sat down, since to his own son the limits of each thing he had told.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Nestor, son of Neleus, sat down again in his place, since he had told his son the limits of every point.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes the speech, and Νηλήϊος is the adjective ‘of Neleus’, in the stock phrase Νέστωρ Νηλήϊος. ἂψ ‘back’ and ἕζετ’ is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’. ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’, not a relative. πείρατ’ ἑκάστου is ‘the limits of each (thing)’, meaning the full extent of every point worth knowing, and ἔειπε is the epic form of the aorist εἶπε.

sentences.t: Μηριόνης δ’ ἄρα πέμπτος ἐΰτριχας ὁπλίσαθ’ ἵππους.
sentences.l: And Meriones then fifth made ready well-maned horses.
sentences.i: Fifth, Meriones made ready his well-maned horses.
sentences.n: Μηριόνης is Meriones, the fifth to come forward. The line is built exactly like line 301, with the same ὁπλίσαθ’ ἵππους ‘made ready the horses’ and ἐΰτριχας ‘well-maned’, with πέμπτος ‘fifth’ in place of τέταρτος.

sentences.t: ἂν δ’ ἔβαν ἐς δίφρους, ἐν δὲ κλήρους ἐβάλοντο·
sentences.l: And they mounted into the chariots, and lots they cast in;
sentences.i: They climbed into their chariots and cast lots;
sentences.n: ἂν … ἔβαν is tmesis for ἀνέβαν ‘went up, mounted’, with ἔβαν the epic form of the aorist 3rd plural ἔβησαν. ἐν … ἐβάλοντο is tmesis for ἐνεβάλοντο, ‘threw in’ in the middle voice: they put lots in a container that the text does not name, to be shaken.

sentences.t:
πάλλ’ Ἀχιλεύς, ἐκ δὲ κλῆρος θόρε Νεστορίδαο
Ἀντιλόχου·
sentences.l:
Achilles shook them, and out leapt the lot of Nestor’s-son
Antilochus;
sentences.i: Achilles shook them, and out leapt the lot of Antilochus, son of Nestor;
sentences.n: πάλλ’ is the imperfect of πάλλω ‘shake’ with the lots as object. ἐκ … θόρε is tmesis for ἐξέθορε ‘leapt out’, the aorist of θρῴσκω without augment. Ἀχιλεύς is Achilles with a single λ, a metrical variant of Ἀχιλλεύς, which the edition prints. Νεστορίδαο is the patronymic ‘son of Nestor’ in the genitive in -αο. The unit ends in the middle of line 354.

sentences.t: μετὰ τὸν δ’ ἔλαχε κρείων Εὔμηλος·
sentences.l: and after him got his place lord Eumelus;
sentences.i: and after him lord Eumelus drew his place;
sentences.n: μετὰ τὸν ‘after him’ means the next lot out. ἔλαχε is the aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’, and the object is understood: the place, or the turn, in the starting line. κρείων Εὔμηλος ‘lord Eumelus’ translates κρείων as ‘lord’ as everywhere.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ Ἀτρεΐδης δουρὶ κλειτὸς Μενέλαος,
τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ Μηριόνης λάχ’ ἐλαυνέμεν·
sentences.l:
and after him next Atreus’-son, famed for the spear, Menelaus,
and after him Meriones got by lot to drive;
sentences.i: and after him the son of Atreus, Menelaus famed for his spear, and after him Meriones drew his place to drive;
sentences.n: The verb ἔλαχε is understood from the previous line for the son of Atreus, and the line then turns to λάχ’ ἐλαυνέμεν ‘got by lot to drive’, an infinitive in -έμεν. δουρὶ κλειτός is ‘famed for the spear’: κλειτός is the same adjective as κλυτός ‘famous’, with the dative of respect δουρί. The lots decide the order of starting places in a line. The unit ends in the middle of line 356.

sentences.t:
ὕστατος αὖτε
Τυδεΐδης ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἐὼν λάχ’ ἐλαυνέμεν ἵππους.
sentences.l:
and last, in turn,
Tydeus’-son, by far the best being, got by lot to drive horses.
sentences.i: and last of all the son of Tydeus, though by far the best, drew his place to drive his horses.
sentences.n: ὕστατος ‘last’ and αὖτε ‘in turn’, with ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἐών ‘being by far the best’ (a concession, ‘though’). The poet notes that the best driver drew the last place. λάχ’ ἐλαυνέμεν repeats the previous line.

sentences.t:
στὰν δὲ μεταστοιχί, σήμηνε δὲ τέρματ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
τηλόθεν ἐν λείῳ πεδίῳ·
sentences.l:
And they stood in a row, and Achilles marked out the turning-posts
far off in the smooth plain;
sentences.i: They took their stand in a line, and Achilles marked out the turning-posts far off in the smooth plain;
sentences.n: στάν is the root aorist 3rd plural of ἵστημι ‘stand’ (Attic ἔστησαν), and μεταστοιχί is an adverb ‘in a row’. σήμηνε is the aorist of σημαίνω ‘mark’, with τέρματ’ ‘turning-posts’. τηλόθεν ‘far off’ places the marks, and λείῳ ‘smooth’ (the same adjective as λεῖος at line 330) describes the plain. The unit ends in the middle of line 359.

sentences.t:
παρὰ δὲ σκοπὸν εἷσεν
ἀντίθεον Φοίνικα ὀπάονα πατρὸς ἑοῖο,
ὡς μεμνέῳτο δρόμους καὶ ἀληθείην ἀποείποι.
sentences.l:
and beside it as a watcher he seated
godlike Phoenix, follower of his own father,
so that he might remember the runs and report the truth.
sentences.i: He set godlike Phoenix beside it as a watcher, the follower of his own father, so that he would remember the runs and report the truth.
sentences.n: παρὰ δὲ … εἷσεν is ‘and beside (it) he seated’, with σκοπόν ‘lookout, watcher’ and ἀντίθεον Φοίνικα ‘godlike Phoenix’. ὀπάονα ‘follower’ is Phoenix’s role, and πατρὸς ἑοῖο is ‘of his own father’ (Peleus); ἑοῖο is the possessive. ὡς μεμνέῳτο is a purpose clause with the optative of the perfect μέμνημαι ‘remember’ (an epic form), and ἀποείποι ‘report’ is the aorist optative of ἀπεῖπον, with ἀληθείην ‘the truth’. The watcher’s job is to witness the race’s result.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἅμα πάντες ἐφ’ ἵπποιιν μάστιγας ἄειραν,
πέπληγόν θ’ ἱμᾶσιν, ὁμόκλησάν τ’ ἐπέεσσιν
ἐσσυμένως·
sentences.i: And all together they raised their whips over their pairs of horses, and struck them with the straps, and shouted at them with words, eagerly;
sentences.n: The race begins. ἐφ’ ἵπποιιν is a dual, ‘over the two horses’, each man with his pair. μάστιγας ἄειραν ‘raised the whips’ and πέπληγον, from πλήσσω ‘strike’, takes ἱμᾶσιν ‘with straps’, the leather straps of whip or reins. ὁμόκλησαν ‘shouted at’ is from ὁμοκλάω, with ἐπέεσσιν ‘with words’, and ἐσσυμένως ‘eagerly’ is from the perfect participle ἐσσυμένος ‘hurrying’. The unit ends in the middle of line 364.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὦκα διέπρησσον πεδίοιο
νόσφι νεῶν ταχέως·
sentences.l:
and they quickly were crossing the plain,
away from the ships, swiftly;
sentences.i: and they were quickly crossing the plain, away from the ships, at speed;
sentences.n: διέπρησσον πεδίοιο is ‘were crossing the plain’, as at 2.785: διαπρήσσω takes the genitive of the ground covered. ὦκα ‘quickly’ and ταχέως ‘swiftly’ say the same thing twice. νόσφι νεῶν ‘away from the ships’ says that the race goes out away from the camp. The unit ends in the middle of line 365.

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δὲ στέρνοισι κονίη
ἵστατ’ ἀειρομένη ὥς τε νέφος ἠὲ θύελλα,
χαῖται δ’ ἐρρώοντο μετὰ πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο.
sentences.l:
and beneath their breasts the dust
stood up, rising, like a cloud or a storm-blast,
and manes streamed with the breaths of the wind.
sentences.i: Beneath their breasts the dust rose and stood in the air like a cloud or a storm-blast, and their manes streamed out on the gusts of the wind.
sentences.n: ὑπὸ … στέρνοισι ‘beneath their breasts’ is the horses’ breasts, with the dative -οισι. κονίη ἵστατ’ ἀειρομένη ‘the dust stood up, rising’ is the formula of 2.150. ὥς τε νέφος ἠὲ θύελλα is ‘like a cloud or a storm-blast’. ἐρρώοντο is the imperfect of ῥώομαι ‘stream, surge’, with μετὰ πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο ‘with the breaths of the wind’ (dative -ῃς, epic for -αῖς), the manes moving as the wind does.

sentences.t:
ἅρματα δ’ ἄλλοτε μὲν χθονὶ πίλνατο πουλυβοτείρῃ,
ἄλλοτε δ’ ἀΐξασκε μετήορα·
sentences.l:
And the chariots at one time on the much-nourishing earth drew near,
at another time darted up, hanging in the air;
sentences.i: At one moment the chariots came down to the earth that feeds so many, at another they darted up and hung in the air;
sentences.n: ἅρματα is plural, ‘chariots’, one for each driver. ἄλλοτε μέν … ἄλλοτε δέ is ‘at one time … at another’. πίλνατο is the imperfect middle of πίλναμαι ‘draw near, come to’, with the dative χθονὶ πουλυβοτείρῃ ‘the much-nourishing earth’, the stock epithet. ἀΐξασκε is an iterative imperfect in -σκε of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, spring’, ‘kept darting up’, and μετήορα is ‘in mid-air’. The unit ends in the middle of line 369.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἐλατῆρες
ἕστασαν ἐν δίφροισι, πάτασσε δὲ θυμὸς ἑκάστου
νίκης ἱεμένων·
sentences.i: and the drivers stood in their chariots, and the heart of each pounded as they strained for victory;
sentences.n: τοί is the article as a demonstrative, ‘those’, and ἐλατῆρες ‘drivers’ is from ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. ἕστασαν is the epic pluperfect 3rd plural of ἵστημι, ‘were standing’. πάτασσε is the imperfect of πατάσσω ‘pound’, with θυμός ‘heart’; the genitive plural ἱεμένων is the present participle of ἵεμαι ‘strain after, long for’, taking the genitive νίκης ‘victory’, and agreeing loosely with the ‘they’ behind ἑκάστου ‘of each’. The unit ends in the middle of line 371.

sentences.t:
κέκλοντο δὲ οἷσιν ἕκαστος
ἵπποις, οἳ δ’ ἐπέτοντο κονίοντες πεδίοιο.
sentences.l:
and each called on his own
horses, and they flew, raising dust over the plain.
sentences.i: and each man called on his own horses, and they flew along, raising dust over the plain.
sentences.n: κέκλοντο is the reduplicated aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘urge, call on’, with the dative οἷσιν … ἵπποις ‘his own horses’; οἷσιν is the possessive, not a relative. ἕκαστος ‘each’ is the subject. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the horses, ἐπέτοντο is the imperfect of πέτομαι ‘fly’, and κονίοντες πεδίοιο ‘raising dust over the plain’ is the same phrase as at 13.820. The part ends with the race in full flight.
